articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says farmers, doctors, teachers shouldn’t be profit-driven: ‘No one ever becomes a …’
articles.summary: Tech News News: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has once again questioned the idea that every profession should be driven by profit, arguing that some of the most importan.
articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has once again questioned the idea that every profession should be driven by profit, arguing that some of the most important jobs in society are built on duty, service and personal commitment. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Sridhar Vembu pointed to farmers, doctors, teachers and priests as examples of professions where money is often not the main reason people choose the work. His comments came a day after he questioned whether society really wants these professions to become profit-driven. Vembu argued that these professions form an important foundation of civilization and that businesses have a role in supporting them rather than treating profit as the only measure of value.Sridhar Vembu says farmers do not choose farming for moneySridhar Vembu began his latest post by asking readers to consider why people choose certain professions. “Ask a farmer who made a choice to be in farming and they would tell you it is their love of farming,” he wrote.He argued that farmers are unlikely to describe money as the main reason they entered agriculture. Instead, he said, farmers may leave the profession when they can no longer afford to continue.Vembu also used doctors as an example. He said doctors are expected to follow professional and ethical rules that put patients first. According to Vembu, doctors who enter the profession mainly for money are not respected by their peers.He made a similar argument about teachers. “No one ever becomes a teacher because the money is good,” Vembu wrote. Vembu also included priests in the same group, arguing that people do not generally train for such roles because they expect financial rewards.Sridhar Vembu says economics may view this behaviour differentlySridhar Vembu then turned his criticism toward economic models. “Economic models would consider all of that behaviour irrational,” he wrote. However, he argued that this willingness to pursue work for reasons beyond money is essential to society. “Yet without that deeply evolved character trait in humanity, civilization itself would collapse.”The Zoho founder's comments build on a broader argument he made in his previous X post about profit, capitalism and society. A day earlier, Vembu had asked: “Do we want our farmers, teachers, doctors and priests to be profit-driven?” He argued that modern finance and economic theory often pushes people toward making more activities profit-driven.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Israeli forces raze West Bank homes as EU weighs ban on settlement goods
articles.summary: Pogroms in the occupied West Bank continue, with Israeli forces demolishing homes and settlers attacking residents.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have demolished more Palestinian homes in the occupied West Bank, as settlers attacked residents of the village of Burqa in an escalation of violence ahead of Israeli elections in October.

The pogroms on Monday came as Ireland pushes for sanctions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements at an informal meeting of European Union ministers this week.

In the town of Birzet, north of Ramallah, Israeli soldiers demolished two residential buildings, saying they lacked the required building permits, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

In Nablus, Israeli forces used a bulldozer to raze a two-storey house and a three-storey building under construction.

And in Burqa, east of Ramallah, video verified by Al Jazeera showed a large group of settlers raiding the village and attacking Palestinians. One clip showed settlers and Palestinians throwing stones at each other.

Witnesses said the settlers entered the village from several directions on Monday night before assaulting residents, trying to set cars alight and stealing livestock.

The United Nations human rights office said last month that settler violence was at an “all-time high”, with new settlements approved and settlers and the Israeli army often acting together against Palestinian communities.

Settler violence and settlement expansion are on the agenda of a two-day meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland beginning on Tuesday.

Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU and has moved to ban settlement goods itself, wants member states to act together.

The talks are expected to build on discussions in Brussels in July, based on a confidential European Commission paper floating three options, including an import licensing system, prohibitive tariffs or an outright ban, according to Reuters news agency.

EU rules require goods from illegal West Bank settlements to be labelled as originating in the occupied territory rather than Israel. But the bloc has not banned trade with the settlements, leaving that to individual states.

Decisions on the policy have long been difficult for the 27 member countries, which are deeply divided over Israel and Palestine.

Neale Richmond, an Irish minister of state, said Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory and its failure to stop settler violence breached international law.

“We see certain EU politicians or European politicians supportive not just of the actions of settlers and settler violence, but of this Israeli government who are supporting them,” he said. “And we cannot be complicit in the actions of this Israeli government, which more broadly is genocidal.”

articles.title: A Missouri man bought the 1914 mansion his late wife had always loved to save it from redevelopment; restoration later revealed $150,000 worth of hidden damage
articles.summary: US News: When Fred Parry’s late wife, Mary, first saw the stately 1914 mansion on West Broadway in Columbia, Missouri, she fell in love. Years later, after her.
articles.body: When Fred Parry’s late wife, Mary, first saw the stately 1914 mansion on West Broadway in Columbia, Missouri, she fell in love. Years later, after her death, Parry found himself facing a choice: let the historic home be redeveloped or step in to save it. He chose the latter, buying the property with the goal of preserving its character and restoring it as a single-family residence. But as crews began peeling back layers of paint and plaster, they uncovered far more damage than anyone had anticipated: rotted framing, compromised structural members and other issues that would eventually add about $150,000 to the restoration bill. His story, as told to the Columbia Business Times, is part love letter to a house, part cautionary tale about historic renovation. Read on to know more:A house tied to a love storyThe mansion, known locally as 'The Belle of West Broadway', sits on a prominent corner just west of downtown Columbia. Built in 1914, it features classic early-20th-century details: tall columns, wide porches, high ceilings, hardwood floors and ornate woodwork that reflect the craftsmanship of the era.For Mary Parry, the house was more than just architecture. She had long admired it and often spoke about how much she loved its design and presence on the street. After she passed away, Fred Parry found himself drawn back to the property, not only as a preservation project but as a way to honour her memory.Buying to save, not to flipWhen the house came up for sale, Parry knew there was interest from developers who might convert it into apartments or split the lot. Rather than risk losing its historic character, he decided to buy it himself with the intention of restoring it as a single-family home and keeping its original footprint intact.His plan was not to create a perfect museum piece, but a liveable home that respected the building’s history while meeting modern standards for comfort and safety. That meant keeping key features, such as the grand staircase, original mouldings and fireplace surrounds, while updating systems like electrical, plumbing and insulation.The moment the real work beganLike many historic renovations, the project started with optimism and a budget based on what could be seen during walkthroughs and inspections. But once contractors began opening walls, removing old additions and stripping away decades of paint and patchwork, the true condition of the house emerged.Crews discovered things like: Rotted wood framing in key structural areas; compromised floor joists and beams that needed reinforcement or replacement;water damage that had spread further than surface signs suggested; and outdated and potentially unsafe electrical and plumbing runs hidden behind walls.What had looked like a straightforward restoration quickly turned into a major structural rehabilitation.The $150,000 surpriseParry estimates that the hidden damage uncovered during restoration added roughly $150,000 to the overall cost of the project. That sum went toward: replacing and reinforcing structural members to ensure the house was sound; addressing long-term water intrusion and moisture issues; and upgrading systems to meet current building codes while minimising impact on historic features.For a homeowner operating on a fixed budget, that kind of mid-project escalation is stressful. But Parry says he never considered cutting corners. “If you’re going to do this, you do it right,” he told the Columbia Business Times, reflecting the mindset of many historic preservationists who see themselves as stewards rather than flippers.Balancing preservation and practicalityRestoring a 110-year-old mansion is not just about fixing what’s broken; it’s about making choices that balance historical integrity with modern living. In the Belle of West Broadway, that has meant: Preserving original woodwork, doors and hardware wherever possible; repairing rather than replacing historic windows when feasible; adding insulation and weatherproofing in ways that don’t damage character-defining features; and designing kitchens and bathrooms that feel contemporary but respect the scale and style of the house.The goal is for the home to function well for today’s occupants while still feeling like a 1914 mansion when you walk through the front door.Why houses like this matterFor Columbia, the Belle of West Broadway is more than one man’s project. It’s part of a small but significant collection of early-20th-century homes that give the city’s older neighbourhoods their character. When houses like this are demolished or radically altered, the streetscape changes in ways that can’t easily be reversed.Parry’s decision to buy and restore the mansion helps keep that architectural heritage intact. It also sets an example for other owners of historic properties, showing that preservation is possible even when the costs and challenges are significant.Lessons for anyone considering a historic homeParry’s experience offers several takeaways for anyone thinking about buying and restoring an older house:Expect the unexpected. Even thorough inspections can miss problems hidden behind walls and under floors.Budget for contingencies. A common rule of thumb is to set aside 10–20% of the projected renovation cost for surprises; in very old homes, that may still be conservative.Work with contractors who understand historic construction. Techniques and materials used a century ago don’t always align with modern building practices, and inexperienced crews can inadvertently cause more damage.Be clear on your goals. Are you aiming for a museum-quality restoration, a comfortable family home with historic character, or something in between? Your answer will guide countless decisions.A home with a futureAs restoration work continues, the Belle of West Broadway is slowly returning to the kind of condition its original builders would recognise, while gaining the updates needed for another century of use. For Fred Parry, the project is both a labour of love and a tribute to his late wife, whose admiration for the house helped set everything in motion.In a time when many older homes are torn down or stripped of their character, this mansion’s survival is a small but meaningful victory for preservation. And for anyone who drives past West Broadway and notices the fresh paint, repaired porches and cared-for gardens, it’s a reminder that behind every historic house there’s often a story of someone who chose to save it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Grey Beard’: 91-year-old man becomes oldest hiker to complete the Appalachian Trail
articles.summary: Dale Sanders says he thanks God and “trail angels” for helping him complete the famed thru-hike. The previous record holder was 83.
articles.body: More than 14 million older adults fall every year in the U.S., perhaps none so often as 91-year-old Dale Sanders. By his count, Sanders fell 71 times while reclaiming his record as the oldest hiker to complete the Appalachian Trail. Six were what he calls hard falls, including one that led to a brief hospitalization and another just 200 yards from the finish. But none were enough to permanently divert him from the 2,193-mile (3,530-kilometer) trail that runs between Springer Mountain in Georgia and Mount Katahdin in Maine. The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines a thru-hike as completing all of the trail’s sections in any order within a year, allowing for pauses. Sanders started September 6 in West Virginia, hopscotched around with some brief breaks and finished Monday atop Maine’s highest peak, where he paused to pray at the sign marking the summit. “I had to thank God, and I had to thank my support team and everybody that got me here,” he said. Sanders, whose trail name is Grey Beard, first set the Appalachian Trail record in 2017 at age 82. Four years later, his 83-year-old friend M.J. Eberhart, aka Nimblewill Nomad, took the title. But within months, Sanders announced his comeback plan. While Sanders’ first journey was easier than he expected, the latest was considerably harder. Despite six months of training, he said he wasn’t in the best condition when he returned to the trail. “And even today, I feel that I should probably be in better shape than I am,” he said last month. “But I just have to always go back and say, ‘But I am 91, so I’m blazing new ground hiking long distances like this.’” In June, Sanders was descending Killington Mountain in central Vermont when he fell forward in a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms and hands. “Thank God nothing got broken, but I was banged up,” he said. “I didn’t rub the blood off, I just kept hiking.” Weeks later, his left arm went numb and he ended up at a Maine hospital. What doctors initially feared was a stroke turned out to be a pinched nerve, but though he was soon cleared to resume hiking, he considered giving up. He returned home to Tennessee in early August to be with his wife, whose mother had just died, and she convinced him to press on. Some of Sanders’ best days were in Pennsylvania, where he enjoyed well-maintained trails and treats delivered by “trail angels.” “When people are taking care of you and bringing you caramel frappes on the trail, the rocks don’t matter,” he said. In fact, Sanders has become something of a star among fellow hikers. Thousands more follow him on social media, which surprised Sanders and caused him to expand his mission beyond reclaiming his record. “I wanna get it back, but right now, that’s secondary,” he said. “Right now, what’s the most important thing - and it’s one of the things that surprised me – is that people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts.” Meredith Ewenson, who met Sanders in June while leading a hike in New Hampshire for 10 other women, said he embodied not just the idea that anything is possible, but that the journey matters most. “Seeing it in real life is something that I’ll definitely remember forever,” she said. Ewenson said her group spotted Sanders early in the morning, but it wasn’t until he blazed by them hours later that they saw the Grey Beard logo on his T-shirt and realized who he was. They caught up with him that night at an Appalachian Mountain Club hut, arriving around 4 p.m. “I got here at noon,” he told them. The next morning, she and others cheered as Sanders performed a “victory dance” before setting off again. “My first thought was ‘Wow, his mobility is insane,’” Ewenson said. “His face on that body just doesn’t make any sense. My brain couldn’t compute how he was so impossibly fit for being that age.” Sanders was born in Kentucky in 1935, two years before the Appalachian Trail was completed. Bullied as a child for his small size, he gained confidence in solo sports like acrobatics and swimming. He later served in the Navy and retired in 2002 after a long career in parks and recreation. Sanders holds numerous other age-related records, including becoming the oldest person to paddle the entire length of the Mississippi River, an 87-day trip he started on his 87th birthday. On his latest adventure, he tackled obstacles like downed trees or steep scrambles with vigor, though he started to get a bit wobbly toward the end of one 12-mile (19-kilometer) day. He laid down on the trail, said he needed a power nap and briefly fell asleep. Two minutes later, he got up and kept hiking.

articles.summary: A Georgia family is demanding justice after police fatally shot their beloved pet donkey, HeeHaw, while searching for a missing child who was later found.
articles.body: A Georgia police officer shot and killed a family's beloved pet donkey after officers searched the animal’s pasture in search of a missing child who was later found at a nearby church. "They claimed he ran up to them braying and they thought they were in danger and shot and killed him after trying to Taze him," Israel wrote on Facebook. A photo taken after the shooting showed Israel crying over her pet donkey, as the animal's eyes remained wide open as it lay lifeless on the ground. "He would normally be standing right over there talking while I'm talking because he thought he could talk like a person could talk," Israel told 11Alive. "Every time he saw somebody, he would run up and bray," Israel said. "And then do a really goofy sound, and because he loved people, and he thought he was a person. He slept in my bed for the first three months of his life," she added. The Cedartown Police Department said the officer who shot the beloved baby donkey has been placed on paid administrative leave. articles.title: Palestine weekly: Israel’s rightwing campaigns on anti-Palestinian abuses
articles.summary: Israeli ministers escalate campaign rhetoric with AI ads as Gaza strikes widen ahead of tight October election.
articles.body:
Ahead of an October election in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is behind in the polls, far-right Israeli ministers have turned the machinery of occupation into campaign material over the last week – not merely as policy, but as the message itself.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose face already appears on campaign billboards across the occupied West Bank, released an AI-generated ad warning that he would do to the Negev and Galilee – areas with large Palestinian populations inside Israel – what he has done to the occupied West Bank by building Jewish settlements there under the slogan “Ahmed is right to be afraid”.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded with his own AI video depicting overweight Palestinian prisoners entering Israeli jails on an assembly line and emerging emaciated and crying. He also published a video of himself berating Palestinian women prisoners and separately planted an Israeli flag on seized United Nations agency for Palestinian refugee (UNRWA) facilities in occupied East Jerusalem.

These were not rhetorical excesses divorced from policy; each echoed recent broader government actions or pressure this week – from seizing a UN facility to a hardening right-wing push for a post-election ground operation to reoccupy Gaza City rather than proceed with Hamas’s disarmament. As the campaign rhetoric intensified, illegal outposts multiplied, demolitions and evictions continued across the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Gaza’s death toll widened again beyond the narrower “targeted assassination” framing to include farmers, delivery workers, fishermen and children.

Gaza’s killings returns to its old shape

Following a brief lull leading up to talks with the Trump-appointed Board of Peace, Israel had framed a return to Gaza strikes around targeting individually named “commanders” of Hamas , though this in practice also included figures from Gaza’s police force.

This week, such pretenses were set aside as the toll widened again to Gaza’s general population. A drone killed three members of the Abdin family while they farmed land in al-Qarara on August 28. Another man was reportedly killed the next day, August 29, near Deir el-Balah. Separate strikes killed at least four people working as delivery drivers or riding electric bikes, and a quadcopter dropped a bomb on children collecting water near a road junction in Gaza City’s historic Tuffah neighborhood.

On August 30, a strike near a bakery west of Deir el-Balah killed Husam Osama Nasir and three-year-old Tim Said Mahmoud Hamdan. On August 31, two Palestinians were killed and several wounded following an Israeli airstrike targeting the entrance of a residential building near the Municipality Park in Gaza City.

Hospitals were hit as well. A drone struck a medicine warehouse inside al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir el-Balah on August 29, wounding three. Hospital officials also reported that cancer medicines had run out entirely after a strike damaged the hospital’s water tanks and laboratory equipment.

Beyond the daily strikes, Israeli journalist Amir Bohbot reported in Walla News that Israel’s military leadership now views a ground operation to reoccupy Gaza City as “unavoidable”. The plan, presented by the chief of the Israeli miltary’s Southern Command which oversees military operations on the Gaza border, would involve evacuating residents to new “humanitarian zones” but is timed for after the October election.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health reported 32 additional deaths last week, bringing the toll since the October “ceasefire” to at least 1,320 by August 31, and the cumulative death toll since October 2023 to 73,456. Some 58 percent of Gaza’s population still faces “critical or catastrophic” shelter conditions, according to the latest humanitarian situation report from the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

In the West Bank, meanwhile, settlers’ efforts to forcefully remove Palestinians from their own homes as part of the ongoing pogrom there continued, including in al-Mughayyir, a village northeast of Ramallah, which soldiers and masked settlers jointly raided on the evening of August 30.

Soldiers shot four residents, sealing the village’s only entrance while settlers besieged a home and loaded stolen property onto a pickup truck.

Beyond al-Mughayyir and Qusra – where Israeli authorities erected three new metal roadblocks encircling the Ras al-Ain hilltop on August 27 – settler violence spanned dozens of incidents this week, according to reports by the Palestinian news agency Wafa and OCHA. In al-Karmel, south of Hebron, soldiers opened fire on a vehicle carrying women home from a wedding on August 27, wounding Sanaa Abu Aram, Doaa al-Hroush and 14-year-old Lana al-Hroush.

In Beita, south of Nablus, settlers attacked and ransacked homes on August 30; Israeli NGO B’Tselem said such vandalism is “routine” and “carried out with the full backing of the Israeli authorities”, with soldiers sometimes participating and other times simply standing by.

Late on August 30, two Palestinians were killed and one detained in an Israeli raid on Nablus city. Elsewhere, among a litany of other incidents in the occupied West Bank, settlers set fire to a grove in Turmus Ayya north of Ramallah, assaulted a former Bethlehem governor, beat two elderly sisters picking figs in Silwad, abducted a British protective-presence activist in Masafer Yatta and stripped gates from Palestinian farmland southeast of Bethlehem, according to Wafa and reports from local activists.

All the while, the Israeli state accelerated the land seizures that Smotrich is now campaigning on. Israel issued a military order seizing land around al-Bireh on the outskirts of Ramallah to encircle the nearby Psagot settlement – illegal under international law – with a “security route”. This is one of 46 such buffer-zone orders issued since October 2023, according to maps and documents shared by the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.

In Nahalin, west of Bethlehem, settlers leveled land to expand Beitar Illit under what a local source said was the direct supervision of the settlement administration. Similar work began near al-Minya to convert an outpost into a full settlement, according to Wafa.

Separately, the Israeli monitoring group Peace Now reported that settlers have established at least 26 new outposts specifically within Area B – nominally under full or partial Palestinian civil administration – over the past two and a half years, with more than 100sq km (39sq miles) now under settler control across Areas A and B combined.

As illegal Israeli outposts were built or expanded, demolitions of Palestinian homes continued. On August 31, Israeli forces demolished two homes in Nablus city and began large-scale demolitions in the al-Saqi area of Birzeit, north of Ramallah, according to Wafa. The commission reported 80 Israeli demolition operations in July alone.

At Qusra, dozens of settlers stormed the besieged area again on August 29, attacking a home under construction with stones. When soldiers arrived some 40 minutes later, they detained and beat the Palestinian residents rather than the settlers, who left without being arrested. Offering rare condemnation of settler violence, Netanyahu called the attackers a “handful of rioters” – but made no mention of the lack of arrests of marauding settlers in the area.

articles.title: Meet Aditi Paudel, a 17-year-old high school student appointed as Japan's first literacy ambassador
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Born in Japan, and raised in Nepal during her early childhood, Aditi Paudel had always shown an affinity towards reading. Her earliest memory of readi.
articles.body: Born in Japan, and raised in Nepal during her early childhood, Aditi Paudel had always shown an affinity towards reading. Her earliest memory of reading is of her grandfather handing her a newspaper filled with intricate Devanagari script when she was still in preschool. But to the surprise of those around her, she was still able to make sense of the text. Over the years, she has only improved and the now 17-year-old high school senior in Tokyo was recently appointed as Japan's first literacy ambassador, as per a report by The Japan Times.The World Literacy Foundation, a global nonprofit headquartered in Australia is running a program where around 900 young people between the ages of 16 and 25 from 101 countries are participating. While the program has been running for 12 years, this is the first time an ambassador from Japan has been appointed, according to Andrew Kay, CEO and founder of the World Literacy Foundation.The aim of the program is to connect young people around the world and get them “involved and waving the flag for literacy in their community,” Kay said, noting that Paudel was singled out “for her leadership, passion for literacy, and commitment to empowering young people in Japan.” “Her curiosity about English shaped thoughtful advocacy, strengthening the program’s global voice and cultural reach,” he added.Paudel returned to Japan to enter the third grade and along with settling into a new life, she found herself having to learn Japanese once more, which meant turning to the books. Her love for reading came pretty early in her life, nurtured by her father who bought her plenty of books. She developed an early taste for fantasy, and recalled falling in love with Enid Blyton’s “The Wishing-Chair.”Reading Malala Yousafzai's autobiography, 'I Am Malala', helped her develop significant interests in female empowerment, including ensuring that women across the world have access to education and literacy. Along with working with children with disabilities, she plans to work with the Shanti Volunteer Association to collect and donate books to Asian countries with lower rates of literacy, including Nepal.With enough experience developing her own reading skills, Paudel said that a common view of literacy is how well a person can read or write, but she sees it in broader terms. Essentially, it’s “something that helps you open doors for more opportunities,” she noted.Paudel has experienced the impact of her access to private education firsthand and how it has set her life on a different course. “My parents grew up in a completely opposite environment. They did not have a childhood like this,” she said. “Being literate is so important because even though you have the potential, you can never unlock it if you do not have literacy.”But even those with easy access to books are reading less than they once did. Around half of elementary, junior high and high school age children in Japan do not read books, according to a recent study by Benesse Educational Research & Development Institute and the University of Tokyo.Fewer young people are reading for pleasure and enjoyment, said Kay, and that could cause a significant regressive effect. “As far as embedding themselves in a novel or reading something that really takes a little bit more effort, that is becoming a rarer thing,” he said. Kay also cautions against the impact of artificial intelligence, noting that the latest tech tools provide quick answers, allowing people to skip the process of researching, reading and wrestling with theories and thoughts oneself.“It’s turning our clock back 150 years … where most people couldn’t read or would have limited ability to read,” he said of the absence of reading books as a mainstream pursuit. Those trends only add importance to initiatives like the World Literacy Foundation’s ambassador program.As a teenager, Paudel understands growing up in a world full of distractions, where much of life is on and from social media. “You will always be more inclined to go for your phone rather than a book,” she said, and because of this, making reading a habit is critical. Her advice for developing a love of reading isn’t about ticking classics off a book list, but finding something that resonates, and that, ideally, can broaden the reader’s perspective.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1968–1969, Robert Redford acquired a Utah ski area and surrounding land amid development pressure; his family later placed 865 acres of wildlife habitat under permanent protection
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Robert Redford saved Timp Haven ski area from development and established the Redford Family Nature and Wildlife Preserve, ensuring the protection of critical wildlife habitats in Utah.
articles.body: In the late 1960s, when Robert Redford turned his attention to Timp Haven, a small ski area in Utah’s Provo Canyon, the surrounding landscape was facing pressure from development. Sundance Institute's corporate archives show that in 1961, Redford first encountered the canyon when he purchased two acres and built a cabin near Mount Timpanogos. Several years later, he acquired thousands of additional acres and, in August 1968, purchased the entire Timp Haven ski operation. The next year, Redford renamed the property Sundance, the mountain resort and community named after his role in the film Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.While modern resort retrospectives simplify this milestone to a single 1969 opening date, a closer cross-reference of land management records and Ski Utah’s historical records mention that he purchased the existing Timp Haven operation in August 1968. Together, the separate records show a transition that unfolded across two years rather than a single transaction in 1969.Redford’s decision to acquire the property was influenced by concerns about how the canyon could be developed. Ski Utah’s history reported that in the late 1960s he acquired around 3,000 acres in an effort to prevent a proposed housing development of A-frame cabins on small parcels from being built in the canyon. Subsequently, he purchased Timp Haven itself and pursued a different model for the mountain, one that included recreation with preservation of the surrounding landscape.From Timp Haven to Sundance Mountain ResortThe Stewart family developed Timp Haven in the 1940s, and the operation expanded over the following years. By the time Redford purchased it, the resort already had lifts and other ski infrastructure. Therefore, his role was not to create skiing in the canyon from scratch, but to take over the existing operations and reshape its future.Redford chose a different approach from intensive mountain development, as he intended to develop little and preserve a great deal. The archives notes that when Redford purchased the land, he redesignated a large majority of it as wilderness preserve. Consequently, the resort’s conservation philosophy developed alongside its recreational infrastructure instead of requiring the ski area to disappear. The institute recorded the 1969 acquisition at 5,000 acres, and the resort subsequently described Sundance as a destination set within those acres of preserved wilderness.The Sundance area lies on the southeastern flank of Mount Timpanogos and contains forests, meadows, wetlands and streams. Furthermore, snowmelt from the mountains feeds waterways that flow toward the North Fork of the Provo River, thus giving the region an important watershed role alongside its wildlife and recreational value.The 865-acre conservation easement by the Redford familyIn 1997, the Redford family donated a permanent conservation easement covering 865 acres to Utah Open Lands. The permanent deed describes the Redford Family Nature and Wildlife Preserve as more than 860 acres of critical wildlife habitat, vital watershed and undisturbed alpine meadows protected in perpetuity.The contract explains that such an easement is different from donating the land itself, as it is a binding legal agreement that restricts development while the property can remain in private ownership. In this case, the easement ensured that the protected acreage's conservation value would remain safeguarded even as ownership or use of its surrounding landscape could change in future.The preserve lies above the Sundance property in North Fork Canyon and includes habitat and watershed resources that the organisation considers important. The protected landscape is reportedly used by wildlife such as elk, mule deer, moose, cougar and black bear, as well as numerous bird species.The protection expanded after the original easementThe conservation efforts by the Redford family continued for decades following the original 865-acre easement. In 2020, Utah Open Lands protected another 316.5 acres through the Redford Family Elk Meadows Preserve. The property reportedly contains year-round moose habitat, important elk habitat, wetlands and areas used by black bears, cougars and coyotes.The latter protection highlights the continuity in the family’s approach to the landscape. The 1997 easement established permanent protection for one major block of habitat, while the later agreement added another area with important wetlands and wildlife habitat.Meanwhile, the resort itself continued to evolve. In 2020, Redford sold Sundance Mountain Resort, and the new ownership vowed to maintain the balance between responsible development and land preservation associated with the resort’s history. The change in ownership did not erase the conservation commitments established during Redford’s tenure. Today, the Redford Family Nature and Wildlife Preserve represents the most concrete permanent protection associated with the family’s early conservation efforts at Sundance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolly Parton estate announces 2-day festival ‘Dollyfest’ to celebrate her legacy
articles.summary: The festival was originally scheduled to take place in January 2026 — around her 80th birthday — and was going to feature Parton as a performer and host. Now, it will serve as a celebration of her legacy.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Dolly Parton is not done yet. The estate behind the icon, who died of cancer last week at age 80, has announced Dollyfest, a two-day festival to be held in Nashville and London across two consecutive weekends in 2027. According to a press release Monday, the festival was originally scheduled to take place in January 2026 — around her 80th birthday — and was going to feature Parton as a performer and host. Now, it will serve as a celebration of her legacy. “We had the venue booked and we had the announcement ready to go. And then, in August 2025, Dolly had to take a step back after her initial health challenges. A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, Dollyfest is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!),” organizer Danny Nozell, founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said in a statement. “We are not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in the ways they choose. However, as far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted,” he continued. “So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.” There was a private service for Parton on Friday attended only by immediate family, The Associated Press has confirmed. There will not be a public ceremony, per Parton’s wishes. Parton’s great-niece, Lainey Parton, posted a tribute on Instagram on Saturday, writing in the caption: “This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words. From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.” Ticket information and dates for Dollyfest are forthcoming.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Edouard forms near Texas and Louisiana while a storm moves toward Hawaii
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Edouard formed Monday in the Gulf of Mexico and was expected to gain strength before bringing heavy rains into parts of Texas and Louisiana.
articles.body: MIAMI — Tropical Storm Edouard formed Monday in the Gulf of Mexico and was expected to gain strength before bringing potentially heavy rains and flooding into parts of Texas and Louisiana. The storm was upgraded Monday night from a tropical depression and forecasters with the National Hurricane Center expect it will make landfall in Texas on Tuesday. Early Tuesday the storm was about 85 miles (135 kilometers) southeast of Cameron, Louisiana, and 115 miles (185 kilometers) southeast of Port Arthur, Texas, with maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (65 kph) while moving west-northwest at 7 mph (11 kph). Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said the biggest problem expected from the storm is flooding. Forecasters are anticipating 3-6 inches (7-15 centimeters) of rain in the greater Houston area, with some areas of the state’s upper coast getting up to 9 inches (22 centimeters). More than 4 inches (10 centimeters) per hour could fall and will likely cause flash flooding in low-lying and urban areas, according to the National Hurricane Center. “This is our first big storm of the season, and I’ll tell you, Texas is prepared,” Orlando Alanis of the Texas Division of Emergency Management said during a news conference. Crews worked Monday to clear dry vegetation that could ignite from a lightning strike and cause fast-spreading fires, Abbott said. Meanwhile, the remnants of Hurricane Dolly brought rain and thunderstorms to parts of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, the Turks & Caicos, and the Bahamas, the hurricane center said. In the Pacific Ocean on Monday evening, Tropical Storm Lowell was about 690 miles (1,110 kilometers) southeast of Hilo, Hawaii, and moving west with maximum sustained winds of 70 mph (110 kph) while moving west at 10 mph (17 kph). Forecasters said Lowell could rapidly intensify and become a major hurricane by Wednesday. Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Karina became a hurricane Sunday, fueled by warm waters far from any shore, and strengthened Monday into a powerful Category 4 storm. But it did not threaten land, forecasters said. On Monday evening, Karina remained a Category 4 hurricane and was centered 1,135 miles (1,830 kilometers) west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico with maximum sustained winds of 130 mph (215 kph) while moving west-northwest at 9 mph ((15 kph), the center said.

articles.title: Could 4+4 make 1 in Libya? UN-backed agreement looks to unite rival camps
articles.summary: After 15 years of civil war, a new UN-backed ‘4+4’ agreement looks to unite Libya’s rival factions.
articles.body:
Representatives of Libya’s rival political camps recently signed a landmark agreement in Tripoli, drafting a roadmap that could see presidential and legislative elections within 24 months.

Mediated by the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), the “ 4+4 committee ” agreement attempts to resolve recurring legal and institutional disputes that have crippled the nation since 2011.

However, in a country plagued by deep mistrust, shifting alliances, and entrenched armed factions, the path from a signed document to a unified government remains fraught with challenges.

Libya has been in a near-perpetual state of instability since a 2011 uprising toppled and killed longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi.

Initially, the country showed political promise, but divisions slowly arose in the rebel camp, chiefly between factions controlling the east and west.

In August 2012, the National Transitional Council officially handed over power to the newly elected General National Congress in what remains the country’s first and only peaceful transfer of power following national elections.

That fragile democratic momentum, however, quickly disintegrated into armed conflict. In May 2014, renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar took control of Benghazi and still controls the east of Libya.

A divisive election later that year prompted some newly announced MPs to form the House of Representatives and relocate to the eastern city of Tobruk under Haftar’s military protection.

The political divide turned into open warfare in April 2019 when Haftar launched an unsuccessful 14-month offensive to capture the capital Tripoli, where the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) was based.

By June 2020, the front lines stabilised near the strategic central city of Sirte, leading to a formal ceasefire agreement later that year that froze military hostilities but left the underlying political fracture intact.

This left Libya with two distinct authorities operating across its territory.

Tripoli is home to the internationally recognised GNA, headed by interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. This western-based authority includes the High Council of State – an advisory legislative body currently led by Mohammed Takala – and the Presidential Council, chaired by Mohammad al-Manfi.

In Tobruk and Benghazi, political power centres on the House of Representatives, led by Speaker Aguila Saleh, which supports a parallel eastern administration. But primary control across eastern and southern Libya is exercised by the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), commanded by Khalifa Haftar.

In recent years, Haftar’s son and LNA deputy commander, Saddam Haftar, has assumed a critical role within the eastern establishment, emerging as the heir apparent, a key military commander, and a central political negotiator.

Despite the 2020 ceasefire, political reunification has remained elusive due to failed international initiatives and systemic economic competition. The 2015 UN-brokered Skhirat Agreement created the GNA.

But it also preserved rival legislative bodies, meaning institutional duplication and the country remaining divided between two powers.

A subsequent UN political track appointed Dbeibah to lead an interim executive in 2021, contingent on conducting national elections at the end of the year.

As part of this deal, Dbeibah agreed not to run, but the 2021 election collapsed just two days before the scheduled vote when he reneged on his pledge.

Another key factor in this new agreement is the involvement of major powers. Under United States President Donald Trump, Washington has intensified efforts to broker a unification deal, led by White House adviser Massad Boulos and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Boulos has put forward an initiative offering US energy investments in Libya’s oil fields in exchange for a unified executive. Washington even proposed a power-sharing arrangement that could see Dbeibah remain as prime minister while Saddam Haftar served as president.

This diplomatic push coincides with an extensive international tour by Saddam Haftar, who has held high-level meetings across regional and Western capitals.

Haftar has held talks with French President Emmanuel Macron and engaged in direct diplomacy with key Arab leaders. Haftar also met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington to discuss institution unification.

Furthermore, regional dynamics have shifted as Turkiye has expanded military and technical cooperation with Saddam Haftar and eastern authorities.

Joint military drills between eastern and western forces in Sirte under US supervision further illustrate this evolving landscape.

The newly signed 4+4 agreement ultimately represents a deliberate attempt to balance power between east and west, analysts say.

The makeup of the committee in its eight members reflects this: Two are from the House of Representatives, two from the High Council of State, and two each from Dbeibah’s government and Haftar’s eastern command.

The agreement mandates presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months under a single executive authority.

It also seems aimed at resolving the primary legal disputes that destroyed the 2021 vote by allowing dual citizens to contest the presidency – so long as the winner relinquishes foreign nationality before taking the oath of office.

Further, it permits military officers to run as candidates upon stepping down from official posts. Both of these legal changes would appear designed to pave the way for either Saddam or Khalifa Haftar, who are believed to have US nationalities and are commanders in the self-styled LNA, to have official government posts.

The deal also restructures the High National Elections Commission under new leadership and establishes rotating official sessions in Tripoli in the west, Benghazi in the east, and Sabha in the south.

Analyst Wissam Abdul Kabir argued that the direct involvement of armed factions distinguishes this pact from previous ones.

“I believe what makes it different is that for the first time, the agreement is signed between the active parties,” Abdul Kabir told Al Jazeera.

“In previous agreements, whether in Geneva in 2021 or the Skhirat agreement in 2015, the agreement was made between the two councils or between the legitimate or elected bodies whose ballot-box legitimacy has eroded over time.

“Therefore, the difference is that the agreement is approved, adopted, and signed by the active parties on the ground, and this is a fundamental point.”

Still, many in Libya view 4+4 as the latest in a series of failed peace initiatives.

High Council of State leader Mohammed Takala boycotted the ceremony, while Presidential Council head Mohammad al-Manfi openly criticised the procedural transparency and foreign involvement in the arrangement.

Mohammed Mahfouz, a political analyst, said the arrangement appears to be nothing more than an attempt by outside powers to cement the powers of Saddam Haftar and Dbeibah.

“The matter goes beyond being confined to the issue of candidacy conditions only. The most important framework is that we are facing a repeated scenario tried in 2015 in the Skhirat Agreement in Morocco, and after that in Tunis and Geneva in 2021,” Mahfouz told Al Jazeera.

“Back then, it was always said that these political agreements take place between active parties … but Libyans did not go to elections.”

Despite the promise of new elections, there is little hope that Libya’s current leaders will relinquish their power if they lose at the ballot box.

“Is it possible to believe the hypothesis that parties possessing power and money, and possessing today new legitimacy according to this agreement and greater authority, will simply accept to be removed from power after two years and lead us towards elections?” said Mahfouz.

“There is a firm conviction among everyone that whoever reaches power in Libya cannot budge an inch from it except by the rifle, unfortunately.”

articles.title: They were building infrastructure in Nepal. Their families in China want to know what happened to them
articles.summary: Chinese workers have been working on infrastructure in Nepal. Their families want to know what happened to them.
articles.body: She kept calling and calling – countless times – but her husband never picked up. The woman, who CNN has given the pseudonym Lili, said her husband had spoken with a friend at 8:27am on Wednesday. That was roughly 10 minutes before an enormous landslide careened down a mountain in Nepal, generating an explosive flood wave that ripped through a border area with China and continued into Nepal. Lili hasn’t heard from her husband, who was working on a Chinese construction project in the South Asian country, since. Hers is one of many families across China desperate for information about loved ones who were in the area when disaster struck, including dozens of Chinese nationals who are believed to have been working across the border in Nepal. Now, these families are wondering whether rescue efforts in Nepal are reaching their loved ones – and are urgently calling for more proactive updates on the progress of those efforts from within China. Several family members of such workers traveled to Lhasa, the capital of China’s Tibetan Autonomous Region, on Monday to seek more information from the state-backed construction firm employing their relatives – and to urge the company to step up rescue efforts and share more information. Families are also asking for local officials in Tibet to help expedite rescue efforts at project sites in Nepal, according to a draft letter to authorities seen by CNN. More than 1,000 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing after Wednesday’s catastrophe, according to authorities in both China and Nepal. Families from both countries – and around the world – are desperate for news of loved ones in the area, which was also a popular route for international tourists. While updates on the numbers of those rescued or confirmed dead have been frequently released on the Nepal side, information has moved much more slowly coming out of China – prompting questions about transparency. Beijing has defended the release of information from its remote disaster area as open and timely. Inside China, news coverage in the country’s tightly controlled media environment has been dominated by state media reports and focused on the efforts of emergency responders at the China-Nepal border area. The experiences of the Chinese families, who are among those waiting for news, have had limited visibility. “Our family is in anguish,” Lili told CNN, adding that her children had stayed in their bedrooms since they learned that their father was missing. CNN is using pseudonyms in order to protect the families’ identities due to the sensitivities of speaking to foreign media. Lili’s husband, who is in his fifties, had been working on the reconstruction of Nepal’s Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi highway, a road stretching through part of northern Nepal to the border with China. Its construction is run by Chinese state-backed engineering firm Tibet Tianlu Company – one of several Chinese firms participating in infrastructure projects across Nepal. After the disaster struck, the company deployed its specialists as well as relief supplies and heavy machinery, while its leadership visited the hard-hit Gyirong port area in Tibet, where rescue efforts are underway, Tibet Tianlu Company said in online statements. But Lili and family members of other workers on that project worry that rescue efforts are being hindered by the location of the project – in Nepal, but close to the Chinese border. “It’s still the families themselves who are organizing and trying to get the rescue efforts moving — going to talk to the (company) leaders, asking them to coordinate with the Nepali government,” Lili said. The sister of another worker on the same highway project told CNN that she believes Nepali rescue workers had not yet been able to reach the area where the project is located. “We haven’t received any information at all … our whole family is extremely worried,” she said. In a draft letter addressed to government officials in Tibet seen by CNN, relatives of 24 of the workers on the highway project expressed concern of a gap in “cross-border rescue efforts.” “Local rescue resources and manpower in Nepal are severely limited and unable to reach the core area to conduct searches. On our side, restrictions arising from the border mean that Chinese rescuers are temporarily unable to cross into the site to carry out rescue operations directly,” said the letter, which CNN has not confirmed was delivered to officials. “We sincerely ask you to understand the families’ anguish… and take concrete steps to get rescue operations underway,” it said. The families also called for authorities to require the company to establish a regular update mechanism for the progress of search and rescue operations, so that “information is transparent and timely.” When reached by phone, a person from Tibet Tianlu’s Board Secretary Office said a team had been set up to handle the situation following the disaster and the company was in touch with families that had arrived at their offices on Monday. When asked about any plans for company rescue efforts on the Nepal side, the person said she “hadn’t received any information” about this. Cross-border disaster Around 100 Chinese nationals are unaccounted for in the disaster-affected area on the Nepal side, according to China’s Foreign Ministry. They are among what Nepali authorities said are more than 500 foreign nationals missing in country overall as of Monday night. China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday said the country was “making every effort to search for and rescue people reported missing both in China and abroad.” All Chinese nationals who had been reached in the disaster zone in Nepal had been safely evacuated, it added, without giving specific number. Chinese workers, as well as official lenders and construction firms, have played a key role in the build-out of Nepal’s roads, hydropower and other projects in recent years, including under the auspices of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s flagship Belt and Road global infrastructure drive. Since the disaster, family members of workers from at least three projects in Nepal, including two hydropower projects, have been in touch with one another, CNN has learned, exchanging information and concerns online – as they await official information. Among them, a man in his 20s CNN is calling Jun said his father had been working at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydroelectric Project in Nepal. The project is one of roughly a dozen hydropower facilities that have become a focal point for rescue efforts. More than 500 workers remained missing at Upper Trishuli-1 as of the latest update from the Independent Power Producers Association Nepal. The project is being built by a Korean engineering firm, with a subsidiary of Chinese state-backed energy giant PowerChina also involved. “What I really can’t understand is why Chinese rescue teams aren’t going over to the Nepalese side to help search for our Chinese nationals,” Jun said. China has sent emergency aid supplies to Nepal and is sharing satellite and hydrological data to aid rescue efforts, as well as providing assistance with DNA identification. Over the weekend, it dispatched nine rescue tunnel experts to the country to advise on efforts to locate workers that may be trapped in hydropower project tunnels. But the lack of information is agonizing for family members like Jun, who said he had last spoken with his father, who is in his forties, during a regular family video call earlier this month. When the mudslide struck on August 26, Jun and his family didn’t pay much attention to the news until the following day, he said, when a labor agency called to tell them that his father went missing. Jun then found his father could no longer be reached by phone. When China for the first time on Sunday opened up two dedicated hotlines for Chinese families seeking information, Jun said he called multiple times, but the line was always busy. He’d already been in touch with the Chinese embassy in Nepal and the hydropower project manager but hasn’t been able to get information about his father’s whereabouts. He said he wants to know the status of the search efforts – “it’s already been such a long time, right? It’s already… it’s the sixth day already,” he said Monday. A ‘timely manner’ That painful count is also being done by families of those who were believed to be at Gyirong port in China when it was hit by a wall of floodwaters on Wednesday morning. The impact obliterated buildings there. No survivors have been reported found since rescue workers arrived Friday afternoon at the port, according to accounts from rescue workers cited by state media. Updates about the missing have been slow to emerge from the area, which cannot be reached by road. The risk of additional flooding and the fact that the area is now covered by thick mud are factors impacting the speed of rescue and recovery efforts there. Information about the area has been dominated by reports from state media, in addition to official government updates. That’s part of a usual playbook by Chinese authorities who look to closely control information flows and ensure data confirmation ahead of its release – part of efforts both to crack down on fake reports and shape public opinion. According to China’s latest update from Sunday, there were 16 dead and 546 people missing on its side of the border. More than 250 foreigners are among the missing, local authorities in Tibet said. Chinese authorities have released new figures on the confirmed dead and missing five times since the disaster, as of Tuesday morning. Independent aid groups are not involved in operations, while foreign journalists are restricted from Tibet without special permissions. CNN is also aware of comments from journalists from outlets that are not China’s national-level official media suggesting they have been barred from reporting in Tibet. Censors have been keeping close watch on online platforms, removing disaster-related videos posted by ordinary users and reprimanding at least a dozen people authorities accused of spreading fake news about the scale of the disaster. During major national incidents, the Chinese government is widely seen as swift to crack down on any forms of dissent or organized efforts to respond or share information outside official channels. In response to a question about assertions that China was not being forthcoming about the scale of the disaster within its borders, a spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday China has been “releasing information openly, transparently and in a timely manner.” But for family members of those who were working in Gyirong port – as with those waiting for information from Nepal – the wait for confirmation of what happened is interminable. Some have taken to social media in recent days to call out for information from any other sources. “Seeking help from locals at Gyirong port,” one person posted on the social media platform RedNote last week. “My cousin, who serves as a border guard there, has been out of contact. What should we do? He has two children at home.”

articles.title: Wendell Berry, Kentucky-born author who advocated a simpler life, has died at 92
articles.summary: Wendell Berry, the Kentucky-born author and agrarian who in poems, stories, novels and essays celebrated the farming communities of his native state and warned of the excesses and misjudgments of an industrial, commercialized society, has died.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Wendell Berry, the Kentucky-born author and agrarian who in poems, stories, novels and essays celebrated the farming communities of his native state and warned of the excesses and misjudgments of an industrial, commercialized society, has died. He was 92. His daughter, Mary Berry, confirmed on Monday that he died in his home in Port Royal, Kentucky. “There’s not enough I could say about him to do him justice,” she told The Associated Press. Few authors were more tied to their home than Berry, an intellectual and spiritual heir to Henry David Thoreau and such Southern agrarians as Robert Penn Warren and John Crowe Ransom. In prose and poetry that mirrored the uncluttered and deeply felt life he advocated, Berry challenged modern assumptions about prosperity and happiness and renewed the mysteries of birth, love, work and death. He had learned from his own history: Berry was born and raised in a farming town during the Great Depression and watched its seemingly immortal ties unravel by his teens. “Increasingly over the last maybe forty years, the thought has come to me that the old world in which our people lived by the work of their hands, close to weather and earth, plants and animals, was the true world,” he wrote in “Andy Catlett: Early Travels,” a novel published in 2006, “and that the new world of cheap energy and ever cheaper money, honored greed, and dreams of liberation from every restraint, is mostly theater.” “The world I knew as a boy was flawed, surely, but it was substantial and authentic. The households of my grandparents seemed to breathe forth a sense of the real cost and worth of things. Whatever came, came by somebody’s work.” Berry was a prolific writer who published more than 40 books, including the novels “Nathan Coulter” and “A Place on Earth,” and the anthology “A Timbered Choir: The Sabbath Poems 1979-1997.” His legacy extended well beyond Kentucky. Michael Pollan, author of such bestsellers as “The Omnivore’s Dilemma,” would say his life was changed by Berry’s declaration that “Eating is an agricultural act.” The chef and food activist Alice Waters cited him as a favorite author and wrote an introduction to Berry’s 1989 essay “The Pleasures of Eating.” He was among the most prominent authors never to receive a Pulitzer Prize or National Book Award, although his honors included a National Humanities Medal and membership in the American Academy of Arts and Letters. In 2016, he was presented a lifetime achievement award from the National Book Critics Circle. A simpler time The tall, slender Berry imagined, chronicled and lived out his vision of a self-sustaining community in which no one had to ask where their food came from or the names of their neighbors. In the classic farming manifesto “The Unsettling of America,” published in 1977, he attacked the consolidation and mechanization of agriculture as a violation of the natural order, whether of the land or of the spirit. “The modern urban‐industrial society is based on a series of radical disconnections between body and soul, husband and wife, marriage and community, community and the earth,” he wrote. “At each of these points of disconnection the collaboration of corporation, government, and experts sets up a profit‐making enterprise that results in the further dismemberment and impoverishment of the Creation.” His disdain for modernity touched upon virtually every aspect of life, from dancing to weather forecasts to birth control, opinions he well knew were not universally shared. Reviewing a Library of America anthology of his nonfiction, The New York Times’ Dwight Garner wrote that Berry “bangs the same themes so relentlessly — the perils of industrial agriculture, the decimation of rural life, America’s blind faith in technology — that one’s eyes begin to cross.” Most of his fiction, closely based on his childhood, was set in rural Port William and populated with such characters as drunken Uncle Peach, the drowned Chicken Little, the wise and patient farm hand Dick Watson and Andy Catlett, Berry’s alter ego, a boy “inclined to be dreamy” and “slide right out of the present world.” His worldview was shaped by an ancient sense of continuity and connection, like in the story “Watch with Me,” when a troubled man known as “Nightlife” picks up an old shotgun and disappears into the woods. A local posse follows, led by the farmer Tol Proudfoot, who worries Nightlife might kill himself or harm others. The pursuit is long and exhausting. “I reckon it would be better not to have got involved,” Tol admits to himself. But he knows that he will continue “until whatever happened that would allow him (Tol) to cease to go along had happened.” “I reckon I am involved,” Tol discovers. Berry yearned for the past but was “painfully divided” by his awareness that “my people established themselves here by killing or driving out the original possessors” and that “people were once bought and sold here by my people.” He saw the U.S. as plagued by “disorderly violence,” and inflamed by the rootlessness of the early settlers and the corporations that followed. “We still have not, in any meaningful way, arrived in America,” he lamented. History led to some controversial opinions — Berry would regard the Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee as more “a tragic figure” than an upholder of slavery — and a clash among Berry, the University of Kentucky and some of its students. Berry’s wife Tanya was the niece of artist Ann Rice O’Hanlon, whose Great Depression era fresco about Lexington history has long been controversial for its alleged sanitizing of slavery. Wendell and Tanya Berry filed a lawsuit in 2020 that objected to its removal from the school. Three years earlier, he had defended the fresco as a painful, but realistic portrait. “Black people did work in tobacco fields,” he wrote. “Black musicians did play for white dancers.” Berry shunned the unnatural world whenever, and however possible. For decades, he and his wife ran a hillside organic farm in Henry County. They lived without computers, television or phones, but did install solar units in 2005, an act of defiance and of commitment to clean energy in a state powered by coal. Well before his lawsuit against the University of Kentucky, his alma mater, he cut ties after the school accepted $7 million for a new basketball dormitory from a group of donors organized by a coal company president. In 2011, he joined a sit-in at the governor’s office in protest of strip-mining. In love with the universe Berry was born in Henry County in 1934, and he moved with his family soon after to New Castle, where his father practiced law and all worked on his grandfather’s farm. As a teenager he graduated from the Millersburg Military Institute and entered the University of Kentucky. In college, Berry helped edit the campus magazine “Green Pen,” read the poetry of T.S. Eliot and Ezra Pound and first encountered the agrarian publication “I’ll Take My Stand.” The 1930 release included contributions from Warren and Ransom among others who would later distance themselves from a racist and romanticized view of the rural South held by many agrarians. By his early 20s, he was publishing poems and stories and even spent time away from Kentucky. He received a Wallace Stegner Fellowship from Stanford University in 1958 and stayed on another year as a visiting lecturer. He also lived in New York, in the early 1960s, but soon purchased Lanes Landing and settled there at the end of the decade. Berry enjoyed the friendship of such fellow writers as Donald Hall and Bobbie Ann Mason, but was inspired more by Kentucky’s land and resources, by the knowledge that he might stand before the same body of water his grandparents drank from. Berry placed himself and fellow humans in a small and blessed role — “sweetly enabled” — within a grand and ordered universe. “And so I go into the woods. As I go in under the trees, dependably, almost at once, and by nothing I do, things fall into place,” he once wrote. “I enter an order that does not exist outside, in the human spaces. I feel my life take its place among the lives — the trees, the annual plants, the animals and birds, the living of all these and the dead — that go and have gone to make the life of the earth.”

articles.title: ‘Not welcome’: How Sweden’s far right took over Stockholm Central Station
articles.summary: The Sweden Democrats also posted advertisements on buses suggesting Swedes with Somali heritage apply for repatriation.
articles.body:
Stockholm, Sweden – When Neira Tokalija, a 39-year-old therapist, saw the slogans of Sweden’s far-right party plastered wall-to-wall across Stockholm Central Station, she felt a familiar sense of fear.

As a child, Tokalija had fled Bosnia and Herzegovina with her family after ethnic cleansing campaigns targeting Bosniaks.

After seeing dozens of campaign posters and installations across Central Station by the Sweden Democrats (SD) , a party with neo-Nazi roots, “it made me feel like it doesn’t matter how much I try as a second-generation immigrant; I’ll never be Swedish enough”, she said.

SD had spent about $100,000 on the station campaign with posters that read “If you commit crimes, live off benefits, don’t learn Swedish or misbehave, you’re not welcome”.

The campaign came weeks before Sweden’s general election on September 13. The SD, which is polling second, could enter government for the first time if the right-wing bloc wins.

The tone of the campaign’s messaging, which ran for one week in mid-August, Tokalija said, evoked a deep historical trauma.

SD also ran several separate campaigns across various Swedish transport networks.

In western Sweden, the party ran provocative advertisements on buses that read: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home.”

The grant, which has been around since the 1980s and was introduced by a Social Democratic government, offered refugees about $1,000 to resettle in their country of origin.

But this year the centre-right coalition government, working with SD, introduced an increase to approximately $36,000 per adult.

About 20 bus drivers with roots in Somalia called in sick in protest.

The public transport operator Vasttrafik removed the posters after the protest, stating that the drivers had been afraid of harassment, and citing risk to the working environment and vandalism.

Zina al-Dewany, a political commentator and editorial writer for the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, told Al Jazeera the plan was to shock.

SD often runs campaigns designed to “provoke a bit too much”, but when they are forced to take them down, the party says it is the “victim”, she said.

After the bus campaign was removed, SD MP Tobias Andersson issued a statement, saying the decision constituted censorship and “election sabotage”.

For decades, Sweden’s political establishment had treated SD as a political pariah.

But after the 2018 general election, a political deadlock prompted right-wing parties to rethink their alliances.

In the following years, meetings between SD and the Christian Democrats and the Moderate Party took place, and in October 2022, the Liberals opened the door to the SD; four right-wing party leaders signed a landmark 62-page contract, known as the Tido Agreement, establishing Sweden’s current coalition government.

In May 2026, another boundary was broken when Simona Mohamsson, the leader of the Liberals and minister for education and integration, announced that her party would allow SD to participate in a future government.

Mohamsson, born in Germany to a Palestinian father and a mother from Lebanon, moved to Sweden when she was eight and is known for her antiracism activism.

After her announcement, Akesson offered a handshake. Mohamsson embraced him, a moment that sent political shockwaves across Sweden.

Many of the staff members who had worked during the SD’s weeklong campaign in the cafes and shops dotted around Central Station believed the audacious campaign was a consequence of years of normalisation.

Ester, a barista, said its scale surprised her, while her colleague Aya said it created “bad vibes” at the station for the week.

The government’s focus on repatriation, coming amid a spate of scandals that dominated Swedish headlines this year, does not sit well with them, they said.

In February, the Swedish Migration Agency ordered an eight-month-old boy born in the country, Emanuel, to be deported alone to Iran while the rest of his family kept their permits.

Around the same time, teenagers who had grown up in Sweden were being told to leave on turning 18 while their parents stayed – a practice the government ultimately suspended in March and moved to reform in June.

One man, who wished to remain anonymous, was working at the station throughout the campaign, collecting money for a charity providing aid to Palestinians in Gaza. He said, although the campaign upset him, he had taken heart from some of the responses.

Angry members of the public had sparked heated debates with the SD representatives at one of their stands inside the station, often centred around its views on Islam and its staunch support for Israel.

Frustrated after the debates, several people handed over large donations to the charity. During the week, it collected far more than usual, the charity worker said.

Al-Dewany also sees some hope. She said the SD has reached a stage of “peak populism”, meaning the party has hit its ceiling. Its focus on immigration while the government was mired in repatriation scandals has started to cost it voters rather than win them, she believes.

Polls in late August put SD on 18 to 19 percent, down from 20.5 percent in 2022.

Tokalija, whose partner and co-parent is from Mozambique, said she was welcomed with “Swedish warmth” and curiosity about other cultures when she first arrived.

Although she still feels this spirit lives on among large sections of today’s society, the rhetoric has changed around immigrants, who are too often painted as “money-seekers”.

Society now demands that families like hers “fully adapt”, she added, stripping away their multicultural and Muslim identities, and leaving a choice between total assimilation and total exclusion, a choice she said mirrors the fascist ideologies she once fled.
