articles.title: UN says areas of Nepal still out of reach as death toll exceeds 1,000
articles.summary: Rescuers are still scrambling to reach some 900 workers believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels. Follow for live updates.
articles.body:
• Death toll: Contact has still not been established with some parts of Nepal’s hardest-hit areas, the UN says, as the death toll following last week’s Nepal-China border flash floods now exceeds 1,000 . More than 4,400 people remain unaccounted for in both countries, according to officials.

• On the ground: Authorities are burying hundreds of unidentified victims in a mass grave, reports CNN’s team in Nepal who also spoke to the man with the Herculean task of reuniting families with the bodies of their missing loved ones.

• Fresh warning: Glaciers surrounding an impact crater in Nepal “may still collapse, posing significant potential risks ,” according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, citing China’s Ministry of Water Resources, which also raised the possibility yesterday.

Nearly a week on from the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border, search efforts are continuing for the thousands of people missing in the catastrophe.

Mourners are also burying their loved ones, with more than 1,000 people confirmed dead in the past week.

Here are some of the latest images from the ground:

A director at the main hospital receiving flood survivors in Kathmandu has said this is not just a disaster for Nepal, but “for the whole world,” as citizens from so many countries are affected.

He told CNN they have treated a total of 72 flood survivors at the hospital, including 33 still being treated. That includes six patients in ICU and 12 patients awaiting surgery.

The wall outside the T.U. Teaching Hospital is covered in posters showing missing people, put up by their families.

They are “searching, searching, searching” between the different hospitals in Kathmandu, hoping for news on their loved ones, Rosyara said.

They are “very sad, very worried, they don’t have their families. They are hurting.”

A CNN team traveled by boat with Nepali police teams searching for bodies washed far downstream by the flood. Here, the Trishuli River is known by a different name, the Narayani, after it merges with another river upstream from the city of Bharatpur.

That city is now the site where hundreds of bodies have been brought as officials work at a painstaking task of identifying them.

The Narayani river is wide and the horizon is flat apart from the green foothills to the north — a world away from the rocky peaks and massive glaciers where the disaster struck almost a week ago. The border with India is about 25 miles away.

The team stopped at one outcrop where the current meets the land and logs and other debris bobbed in the water. They got off and probed the tall grass with sticks, but found no bodies.

They did the same at a small island further downstream, where they said they had previously found several bodies. None were found, but a rotting animal carcass stench was in the air.

When each team had finished searching an area, they blew a whistle to signal the all clear and the journey began again.

These teams have been on the river for days, pulling decomposed bodies from the water.

“The smell of death stays with you,” one member of the recovery team told CNN.

“Everyone feels heavy when they see the dead bodies,” said another.

“These scenes are very heart-wrenching,” the recover team member said. “But … if we feel weak, we can’t work. … We are keeping ourselves strong and working.”

At least 1,003 people have died in the floods in Nepal, the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said earlier today.

This brings the total number of deaths on the Nepal-China border as a result of the floods to at least 1,019.

Contact has still not been established with some parts of Nepal’s hardest-hit areas after last week’s flooding, according to a UN report.

Glaciers surrounding an impact crater in Nepal “may still collapse, posing significant potential risks ,” days after the floods, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, citing China’s Ministry of Water Resources.

China will send DNA identification experts to Nepal , foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a regular press briefing today.

Chinese state media reports that a single water tower higher up in the mountains is the only structure still standing in the Gyirong port area that was devastated by massive flood waters almost a week ago.

The risk posed by one of the key barrier lakes formed after last week’s catastrophic flooding is now “under control” with all of its water discharged, Chinese authorities said today.

CNN’s Billy Stockwell, Sylvie Zhuang and Lauren Kent contributed to this reporting.

More than a thousand people have been killed and thousands more are missing in Nepal and China due to catastrophic flooding in the cross-border region.

Here’s a look at how the situation has developed since the flooding began last week:

At 8:37 a.m. Nepal local time on Wednesday (10:52 p.m. Tuesday night ET), shaking is reported by the US Geological Survey (USGS) along the Nepal-China border, north of Kathmandu. Around this time, an “avalanche” of ice and rock tears down a mountainside and into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, which flows from China into Nepal.

Just before midday local time (around 2 a.m. ET), Reuters reports “a massive flash flood in the Himalayan nation of Nepal.” Roughly two hours later, the country’s national police force reports at least eight deaths as a result.

By 2:45 p.m. local time (around 5 a.m. ET), Nepal’s Tourism Board says that at least 384 travelers, including 291 foreign nationals, are considered missing. The Red Cross deploys an emergency team to affected areas, its regional office says.

At 5:55 p.m. local time (8:10 a.m. ET), CNN reports that the death toll in Nepal has risen to at least 17. Less than 25 minutes later, this toll increases to 31 . By 11:08 p.m. local time (1:23 p.m. ET), at least 157 people have been reported dead in the flash floods, Nepal Police says.

The number of people reported missing on the Chinese side of the border rises to 558 , according to the local government in the city of Shingatse.

The death toll in Nepal rises to 162 , then 270, then 353 , then 389 throughout the day, according to the country’s police.

Rescuers in India recover three bodies in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh, with Reuters reporting that raging waters are suspected to have carried mud-covered remains downstream into the country from Nepal.

The US State Department says that 90 Americans who may have been impacted by the Nepal floods are unaccounted for.

The death toll in Nepal once again climbs to 469 , then 489 , then 538, then 579 , according to the national police force.

A barrier dam lake on the Chinese side of the border bursts its banks, forcing rescue efforts to be paused. They are resumed hours later.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang laments the “significant loss of life” caused by the flooding, with at least five dead and 550 missing in his country.

By Saturday morning local time, the death toll in Nepal has risen to 616 , according to the national police. Throughout the day, this jumps to 626 , then 675.

Local police tell CNN that officials in the central Nepali district of Chitwan are planning to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies in a mass grave at a sacred Hindu site.

One of two new lakes that have formed near a flood zone along the Nepal-China border has “essentially drained,” China’s state broadcaster CCTV reports.

The death toll in Nepal rises to 734 , then 762 , then 788 , according to Nepal Police.

Meanwhile, the death toll in China rises to 16 , while the number of missing falls to 546, state broadcaster CCTV reports.

An estimated 898 workers at various hydropower projects in Nepal are unaccounted for, according to the country’s Independent Power Producers’ Association. Rescuers undertake urgent efforts to pump air into a tunnel at a hydropower project along Nepal’s Trishuli river.

The death toll in Nepal rises to 903 , then 939 , with approximately 3,925 people missing. This brings the total number of people missing in Nepal and China to 4,471.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah says that more than 11,000 people have been rescued since the flooding began.

A State Department spokesperson says that approximately 80 Americans remain missing in “the Nepal/China cross-border region.”

CNN’s Laura Paddison, Billy Stockwell, Sugam Pokharel, Max Saltman, Sylvie Zhuang, Sophie Tanno, Amarachi Orie, Jennifer Hansler, Bhadra Sharma, Lex Harvey, Nishant Khanal, Sana Noor Haq, Kara Fox, Laura Sharman, Sangi Gurung, Simone McCarthy, Jessie Yeung, Kathleen Magramo and Anup Pradhan contributed to this reporting.

Contact has still not been established with some parts of Nepal’s hardest-hit areas after last week’s flooding, according to the United Nations.

Major road and bridge damage — which may take weeks to fix — is restricting access, a UN report says.

The report, published Monday and produced by the Office of the UN Resident Coordinator in Nepal, sets out various humanitarian needs across the country’s north in the aftermath of the deadly flash flooding.

What else is in the report? Among the wide-ranging humanitarian challenges, it said some 2,600 children under the age of five, out of an estimated 22,100 affected children, are expected to require treatment for “severe wasting,” while thousands of pregnant women require nutritional support.

Surveillance is needed to track the potential spread of diseases, including cholera, malaria and typhoid fever, among others, the report states.

The report said more than 100 children may have been separated from their parents or caregivers, citing “preliminary reports.” Meanwhile, at least 19 schools have been damaged due to the flooding, the report said.

Glaciers surrounding an impact crater in Nepal “may still collapse, posing significant potential risks,” days after the massive deadly floods in the Himalayan region, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, citing China’s Ministry of Water Resources.

The warning marks the second consecutive day that the ministry has raised the possibility of the glaciers collapsing.

The Chinese state broadcaster previously reported that areas of standing water near the mountainside impact crater, which was formed by the glacial collapse last week, were “in a state of overflow.”

Based on new drone footage taken Tuesday morning, the Chinese ministry assessed that the water accumulated in the impact crater of Nepal’s Chhochen Khola River has “basically drained,” and the downstream river is flowing normally. However, the risk of glacier collapse remains, the ministry warned.

CNN’s Fred He contributed to this report.

More than a thousand people have died since catastrophic flooding hit the Nepal-China border region last Wednesday, with thousands more reported missing.

Here’s a look at the disastrous impact of the flooding in numbers:

At least 1,003 people have died in the floods in Nepal, the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said in its latest update a short while ago.

A further 3,916 people are missing in the catastrophe, the NDRRMA said.

Some 583 foreign nationals are among the missing, the Nepal Tourism Board said in a statement yesterday.

Another 315 foreign nationals have been rescued, the tourism board said, including people from India, China, Germany, Bulgaria, Turkey, Italy, the United States, Malta, Switzerland, Russia, Portugal and Oman.

A further five foreign nationals are in contact with authorities, the tourism board said, three of which are Spanish, one Belgian and one from the US.

At least 11,379 people have been rescued since the flooding began, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said yesterday .

At least 16 people have died in the flooding in China, state broadcaster CCTV reported Sunday morning local time.

At least 546 people are also missing in China, CCTV reported.

Among the missing are at least 261 foreigners from 23 countries , authorities said during a press conference Sunday.

Of those missing, 104 are from Nepal, 49 are from India, 33 are from Latvia, 18 are from the United States, and 15 are from the United Kingdom, Chinese authorities said.

Foreign nationals from Canada, Australia, South Africa, Russia, Malaysia, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Estonia, France, Ireland, Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain, Hungary and Kazakhstan are also missing, Chinese authorities said yesterday

CNN’s Bhadra Sharma, Simone McCarthy, Laura Sharman, Billy Stockwell, Anup Pradhan and Kosh Koirala contributed to this reporting.

Chinese officials briefly paused their rescue mission last week due to worries of flash flooding when water in the lake began overflowing.

The Purepu Tsangpo barrier lake has now “fully discharged its water, with the risk under control,” China’s state broadcaster CCTV said, citing emergency officials.

The assessment was based on observation posts, video surveillance, slope radar monitoring and early warning systems focused on the lake, CCTV said.

Some context: A barrier lake is a body of water created by debris damming up a river. They can pose major risks of flash flooding if water behind those dams suddenly releases.

She kept calling and calling – countless times – but her husband never picked up.

The woman, who CNN has given the pseudonym Lili, said her husband had spoken with a friend at 8:27am on Wednesday. That was roughly 10 minutes before an enormous landslide careened down a mountain in Nepal, generating an explosive flood wave that ripped through a border area with China and continued into Nepal.

Lili hasn’t heard from her husband, who was working on a Chinese construction project in the South Asian country, since.

Hers is one of many families across China desperate for information about loved ones who were in the area when disaster struck, including dozens of Chinese nationals who are believed to have been working across the border in Nepal.

Now, these families are wondering whether rescue efforts in Nepal are reaching their loved ones – and are urgently calling for more proactive updates on the progress of those efforts from within China.

Several family members of such workers traveled to Lhasa, the capital of China’s Tibetan Autonomous Region, on Monday to seek more information from the state-backed construction firm employing their relatives – and to urge the company to step up rescue efforts and share more information.

Families are also asking for local officials in Tibet to help expedite rescue efforts at project sites in Nepal, according to a draft letter to authorities seen by CNN.

More than 1,000 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing after Wednesday’s catastrophe, according to authorities in both China and Nepal. Families from both countries – and around the world – are desperate for news of loved ones in the area, which was also a popular route for international tourists.

Authorities are burying hundreds of unidentified victims after catastrophic flooding overwhelmed morgues and left families unable to reach loved ones. CNN’s Hanako Montgomery reports.

The number of people killed in last week’s devastating landslide and flash flooding in Nepal and China has topped 1,000 as of Tuesday morning, according to authorities.

As rescue efforts continue for the more than 4,400 people still missing, our teams on the ground in Nepal are telling the heartbreaking and resilient human stories amid scenes of death and destruction.

• Resilience in the air: Priya Adhikari, Nepal’s first female helicopter pilot, has flown around 100 missions in less than a week, to rescue survivors from hard-hit areas. She spoke to Anderson Cooper about the search effort and what keeps her going.

• A miraculous rescue: 5-year-old Manisha Magar was presumed dead after she was swept away by the catastrophic flooding. Then, her parents saw video footage of her rescue. CNN’s Will Ripley caught up with the family in Kathmandu.

• A difficult reunion: Our reporters spoke to a man in Nepal facing the Herculean task of reuniting families with the bodies of missing loved ones — but after days in the river, many are in a condition making identification difficult. CNN’s Hanako Montgomery reports from a mass burial site where authorities are laying to rest hundreds of unidentified victims.

• Families seek answers: Family members of missing foreigners, a figure which includes about 80 Americans, have travelled to Nepal to search for their loved ones. Anderson Cooper spoke with an American doctor who is looking for her parents. “Our hope is that if they heard the alarms and the warnings, they either drove or they ran,” the doctor said.

articles.title: She was a ’90s grunge queen. These are her photos on the road
articles.summary: Bassist Melissa Auf der Maur toured with Hole and the Smashing Pumpkins during a whirlwind decade she documented on film. But she held onto the photos in private, until now.
articles.body: If Courtney Love was the unpredictable fire of Hole, bassist Melissa Auf der Maur was her cool counterpart, the frontwoman’s right-hand woman both on and off the stage. For five years, the Montreal-born Auf der Maur joined the grunge-rock act just as they crested toward a vertiginous, yet precarious peak, shortly after the release of their explosive album “Live Through This.” The album came out one week after Kurt Cobain, Love’s husband, shocked the world with his suicide, and two months before Kristen Pfaff, the band’s founding bassist, died by overdose. The seismic cultural shift by Cobain and Nirvana — along with bands including Soundgarden, Pearl Jam, and Alice in Chains — ushered the underground into the mainstream and has yet to be replicated since. The period was captured on MTV, VH1 and radio; on analog cameras for music magazines and videotapes now archived as grainy clips on YouTube. And as the period recedes further in memory, the gatekeepers are fewer, too. At 54, Auf der Maur is now offering her own account, a vast but rarely seen archive captured on point-and-shoot film cameras. The forthcoming book, “My ’90s Rock Photographs,” brings together more than 200 images of the bassist’s life on stage, backstage, on the road and in hotel rooms, as she both documented the alternative renaissance she was part of and kept up with the artistic photography practice she had originally intended to be her career. It accompanies an exhibition this September at The Art Gallery of Ontario and a future feature-length documentary film about her archive. It also follows her release of a tell-all memoir, as well as a batch of early demos, all in the same calendar year. It’s what Aur der Maur calls her “21st-century midlife resurrection.” “2026 is definitely my purging of the ‘90s, but also my healing of a decade that made and broke me,” the musician and artist explained from her home in New York’s Hudson Valley, where she’s lived since 2008 and where she co-founded the arts center Basilica Hudson with her husband, filmmaker Tony Stone. Reclining on her couch over a Zoom call, she reflected on the time that’s passed since her five-year stint with Hole, followed by a year with The Smashing Pumpkins for their farewell tour — a decade of exhilaration and excess and tragedy all at once. “It’s (been) enough time for healing to happen, but also a good amount of time for clear perspective on how it sits in the big, big picture of human history.” Across the book, we follow Auf der Maur as she is thrown into the fray, as an aspiring artist who studied photography but was pulled into Love’s magnetic orbit by way of the musician Billy Corgan (Auf der Maur’s own band Tinker opened for his band, The Smashing Pumpkins, in 1993 thanks to her fan letter to him). She snaps photos backstage at Saturday Night Live, where Hole performed the furious anthem “Violet” during a holiday episode in 1994; and from balcony seats during Nine Inch Nails’ “Self-Destruct” tour, which they opened for a handful of dates before Love’s infamous fall-out with the industrial act’s frontman and founder Trent Reznor. She describes in the book the experience of being onstage with Hole as a battle, like ancient Roman gladiators. But off-stage they were silly, and messy, and real. She photographs Love against a sea of thousands of fans, smiling wide with ruby-red lips and a slice of cake, and with Auf der Maur in a limo to the 1995 MTV Awards, Love and Cobain’s daughter Frances Bean stretched across their laps. For Auf der Maur, part of the work of unearthing her archive has been to advocate for Love while still acknowledging the problems she had. “It’s very much enforced by the memoir, too, but I absolutely give a f**k of a lot of time to reframe Courtney as one of the most misunderstood women in history,” she said. “(It’s a) very solid, lucid perspective of what the world did to her, while also telling the truth.” Returning and reconnecting Across her images, Auf der Maur reckons with fame and performance and visibility in different ways. Sometimes, her documentation is simple and lighthearted, taking selfies and portraits with other stars in her orbit, from Danny DeVito to Drew Barrymore and Chloe Sevigny. But the period was tumultuous, too. Love battled addiction and faced endless scrutiny from the media, drummer Patty Schemel — Auf der Maur’s closest bandmate — struggled with her own drug problems, and Auf der Maur lost her father just before the release of the 1998 album ‘‘Celebrity Skin.” In the book, she intersperses photos of that time, of her ill father, his funeral, and the things he left behind. After the musician quit touring in the early 2000s, she put down both her instrument and her camera. For the first decade of her daughter River’s life, the child didn’t know her mother was ever in a band; but the talk became unavoidable when other parents would tell her that they saw her mother on stage in her ’90s heyday. Auf der Maur only seriously began to revisit her archive once she’d turned 50 and River was nearing her teenage years. “I needed that much time to be able to look at the death of my father, look at the life of extreme pain, drug addiction, death that I was bathed in in my 20s,” she said. “I needed to grow as a human and become a mother and stop making music and get off the road, so that I could be strong enough to look at the hard parts and to celebrate the things that I couldn’t have seen then.” Returning to her photographs meant returning to a much earlier version of herself, too: the artist who had originally said no to joining Love’s band because she felt she was meant to get her master’s in photography instead. Auf der Maur had looked to the self-portrait practices of women photographers like the late Francesca Woodman and had been developing a visual language of her own, which can still be seen in a more transitory state in hotel rooms as Auf der Maur turned the camera on her own body. “I thought I was going to be a fine-art photographer who had my own practice, which was rooted in self-portraiture and reflection of time and the feminine body,” she explained. “I figured that’s what my life was going to be, but then overnight, like literally, grunge Cinderella.” She found herself documenting everything, every day, but at the time she couldn’t put the full ‘why’ into words. “I just knew that history was happening, and I knew I was just like a servant to our generation.” “This was not about me — even though, yes, I took a lot of photos of me,” she continued. “I was trying to also capture (being) a woman in a rock band, but also a woman in my generation watching our magic be co-opted by corporate machines and ripping our souls out.” For a long period, she and Love fell out of touch, but have reconnected over time. And in the process of writing her memoir, she said she received the blessing of all of her former bandmates. She believes the reason why she’s had their support is a deep sense of trust, that Auf der Maur “doesn’t give a f**k about money, fame, or power,” she said. “That is not why I exist, nor what I call to. In fact, I run away from that quite often. If anything, I’m trying to elevate our higher selves.” Her renaissance year is continuing in full force. She’s teased reunions on stage with Love, and joined The Smashing Pumpkins as a guest onstage at Lollapalooza alongside Olivia Rodrigo — one of River’s favorite artists, who joined her on the trip to Chicago. “She’s only getting to know that part of me now,” she said, smiling. “It was a full-circle dream for her to see her mother get aligned with things that she likes. She and her friend took an entire suitcase of my ’90s clothes to incorporate in their Lollapalooza weekend outfits, and that’s when I thought, ‘OK, I really, I really, I really made it now.’”

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was asked to name the smartest person he has met; his unexpected answer may change how we see intelligence
articles.summary: Have you thought about it? What does it mean to be smart in this day and age? Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, the world's most valuabl.
articles.body: Have you thought about it? What does it mean to be smart in this day and age? Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, the world's most valuable tech giant powering the artificial intelligence revolution, was asked the same question.“Who's the smartest person you've ever met?”Earlier this year, the tech giant with 33 years of experience, the single-longest-serving chief executive in the S&P 500, was met with this question. He was asked this on the podcast A Bit Personal with Jodi Shelton. For a driven and visionary boss like Huang, that’s the kind of question that would jolt the memory and lead to an anecdote. But contrary to what one may assume, the Nvidia boss found this question impossible to answer. His answer went sideways in the best possible way!"I can't answer that question," he said. Then he explained why, and in doing so, he explained how AI is reshaping the way we measure human intelligence and value.AI is changing the definition of ‘smart’“Who's the smartest person you've ever met?” Jodi Shelton asked. If she had asked this question at least half a decade ago, Huang would have answered instantly. But with the evolution of artificial intelligence, everything is different. “The definition of smart is somebody who's intelligent, solves problems, technical. But I find that that's a commodity. And we're about to prove that artificial intelligence is able to handle that part easiest, right,” the Nvidia CEO said.He also shared an example that would help explain it better. “Everybody thought software programming is the ultimate smart profession. Look, what is the first thing that AI is solving? Software programming,” he said.With AI, everything changed. Code completion tools can now write code. AI systems debug. The profession that once required peak intelligence is now commodified, accessible and insanely fast. The real question is: if programming falls this quickly, what doesn't?Jensen Huang emphasised that the ‘definition of smart is very different from what most people think’.What does it mean to be ‘smart’ in the AI age?For decades, we've optimised everything around training people to solve defined problems efficiently. Schools, universities and hiring systems all worked for that. Now those skills have lost their charm. According to Huang, a smart person today is someone who is technically astute, but also has empathy, the ability to read what isn't said, and the capacity to sense around corners.“I think, long-term, the definition of smart and my personal definition of smart, is someone who sits at that intersection of being technically astute, but (with) human empathy and having the ability to infer the unspoken around the corners, the unknowables.”"People who are able to see around corners are truly, truly smart," he said. "And their value is incredible.”He calls this skill or instinct ‘feeling the vibe’. “To be able to preempt problems before they show up, just because you feel the vibe.”And this vibe isn’t really one thing, according to Huang. It's a form of intelligence nearly opposite to what we've been training for all this while. “And the vibe came from a combination of data analysis, first principles, life experience, wisdom, (and) sensing other people. That vibe, that I think, that's smart. That, I think, is going to be the future definition of smart,” he explained.So the smart person in today’s era should be able to recognise patterns at a human level, take intuitive leaps, and also have the ability to operate in ambiguity. And machines cannot do any of this, not yet. They can process data and find patterns. But they can't feel the room. That is where human intelligence is crucial. They can't know what matters when the criteria keep shifting. They can't navigate the unknowable. But humans can. And those who can are the smartest.Huang also shared the sharpest insight. The kind of smartest person he described may not necessarily tick all the boxes of the conventional metrics used to evaluate intelligence. “And that person might actually score horribly on the SAT,” the Nvidia CEO said.The most intelligent people in this AI age are not the ones with the most technical skills, but those who bring something AI cannot easily replicate.Looking for trusted parenting advice? Follow TOI Parenting Circle on Instagram for expert guidance, relatable stories, and practical tips delivered every day.

articles.title: NJ boater faces homicide charge as deadly summer on the water claims another life in third fatal crash
articles.summary: Kevin Wells faces vehicular homicide charges after his boat struck a channel marker in Barnegat Bay, killing a 26-year-old passenger aboard.
articles.body: A New Jersey man faces felony charges following a late-night crash in Barnegat Bay that killed a 26-year-old passenger and left two others critically injured along the Jersey Shore in late July. Troopers from the New Jersey State Police Marine Bureau arrested Kevin Wells, 40, of Warren, New Jersey, on Friday, charging him with vehicular homicide and two counts of assault by vessel while intoxicated. State police said troopers responded just before 11 p.m. on July 25 to reports of a serious vessel collision along the Intracoastal Waterway in Toms River Township. UNLICENSED NYC BOAT OPERATOR ALLEGEDLY IGNORED SAFETY WARNINGS BEFORE MOTHER, BABY DIED IN CAPSIZING: FEDS Investigators said Wells was operating a 32-foot Boston Whaler through the waterway when the boat struck a channel marker. Following the impact, Wells navigated the damaged vessel to a private residence on Silver Lagoon Drive in Toms River Township, where emergency personnel arrived to render aid. A passenger aboard the boat, Michael T. Bereheiko, 26, of Green Brook, New Jersey, was rushed to an area hospital, where he later died. Two other passengers – 27-year-old Steven Pochick, of Green Brook, and 27-year-old Nicholas Cherasaro, of North Plainfield – sustained serious injuries and were transported to a local hospital. A fourth passenger, 24-year-old Sarah Stulh, of Bayville, suffered minor injuries. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X According to his obituary, Bereheiko was a 2017 graduate of Watchung Hills Regional High School, where he played varsity football on both offense and defense. Teammates affectionately called him "Bear." He later attended Lincoln Tech, studied to become a heavy diesel mechanic and worked for Schifano Construction Corporation in Middlesex. articles.title: Abroad and at odds: How the war has divided Iranians in the diaspora
articles.summary: Many Iranians in the diaspora remain caught in the paradox of opposing  the war and the government in Tehran.
articles.body:
Peyvand Khorsandi was only four years old when he and his family left Iran for the United Kingdom in 1976, three years before the Islamic revolution .

His father, Hadi, a well-known Iranian satirist and poet, was the target of a failed assassination attempt, allegedly orchestrated by the Iranian government in 1984. The attack was foiled by London’s Metropolitan Police following a tip-off from a senior Iranian official, who soon went into self-imposed exile.

Despite that history, Khorsandi still opposes the US-Israel war on Iran and says it has granted the government a new lease of life while delivering a serious setback to pro-democracy Iranians.

“It’s disappointing and depressing,” he told Al Jazeera.

Khorsandi is one of many Iranians in the diaspora caught in the paradox of opposing both the government and the war on Iran.

The conflict, which began six months ago on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran, has upended the global economy, caused energy prices to spiral and killed thousands of civilians, mostly in Iran and Lebanon.

The region is stuck at a crossroads of continued uncertainty, and the war has left the Iranian diaspora divided, with many in Western countries supporting the attacks on their ancestral homeland, and others opposing the war.

Supporters of the strikes have mostly rallied around Reza Pahlavi , the son of Iran’s deposed shah, or king. Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi was toppled in 1979 following decades of rule.

Others, like Khorsandi, reject Pahlavi’s politics.

“What Pahlavi supporters represent is dangerous. I think he [Pahlavi] is a willing servant of the Israeli government,” Khorsandi told Al Jazeera.

“Like Iraq, this is a racist war. The lives of Global South people are expendable. We are as expendable to them [the US and Israel] as Palestinians. It’s a war fought for colonial sensibilities. Some diaspora Iranians made the mistake of thinking that the West sees them as equals.”

Humanitarian case for attacks begins to unravel

The US-Israel war on Iran is widely seen as a one-off choice. US intelligence had already concluded that Tehran was not trying to weaponise its nuclear programme before the conflict was launched.

Nevertheless, US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attempted to justify the conflict at the outset on human rights grounds, suggesting that they sought to help common Iranians. However, that argument began to unravel just a few hours into the war when an elementary school for girls in the southern city of Minab was bombed.

At least 170 people were killed in Minab, most of them children. Evidence examined by news outlets and rights groups overwhelmingly suggests that the school was hit by a US air strike . Pahlavi failed to condemn the attack and said Tehran was to blame, accusing the government of using the victims as “human shields”.

“It has created a lot of discord,” Khorsandi said.

Netanyahu remains the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for war crimes and crimes against humanity over Israel’s war on Gaza, which an independent United Nations inquiry has concluded amounts to genocide.

Meanwhile, Iran’s human rights record remains abysmal. Amnesty International has accused Tehran of exploiting the war to carry out “systematic repression”.

The rights group says thousands of people have been arbitrarily detained, including activists, protesters, journalists and lawyers, among others. It alleges that forced confessions have been used in “unfair sham trials”.

The latest US intervention in Iran has reminded many Iranians of Mohammad Mossadegh’s legacy, the country’s democratically elected prime minister, who was overthrown in a coup masterminded by the CIA and MI6 in 1953. The US and British intelligence agencies conspired to remove Mossadegh after he nationalised Iran’s vast oil reserves, which were controlled by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, now named BP (British Petroleum).

Former US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright acknowledged in 2000 that the US had played a “significant role” in the coup, describing it as “a setback for Iran’s political development”.

According to the Roosevelt Institute for American Studies in the Netherlands, Mossadegh’s ousting helped shape “the environment in which the Iranian revolution of 1979 was able to take hold”. Iran has been heavily sanctioned since then, going from a key US ally to an archenemy.

The impact on the economy has been catastrophic, with common Iranians bearing much of the cost. The international isolation has left many in and outside the country disillusioned, while the government’s repression has further fuelled discontent and a desire for change.

“There were those inside Iran who believed Trump would really bring help. There were similar aspirations and hopes on the part of those in the diaspora who supported the war. And I think in many cases, they’ve been disappointed,” Roxane Farmanfarmaian, who teaches international relations of the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) at Cambridge University, told Al Jazeera.

“I think there’s very little expectation at this point that, should there be a change of government in Iran, the diaspora would see eye to eye across its different groups,” she added.

Naz Radboy’s parents are Iranian. She was born in the US and splits her time between there and the UK. Despite not growing up in Iran, she maintains deep ties to the country. For her, the war is a form of US imperialism against a government that refuses to bow to Washington.

Radboy supports the country’s leaders and says she has paid a heavy price for doing so.

“Iran is confronting [the] empire, and I stand with Iran and the institutions defending it,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Iran does not exist in a vacuum. It exists inside an international order dominated by an empire that has surrounded the region with military bases, imposed devastating sanctions, carried out regime-change operations across the Global South and repeatedly asserted its right to determine which governments are legitimate. So when Iran builds the capacity to resist that order, I understand why.”

The war remains deadlocked. Despite overwhelming US military power, Iran still controls traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which has emerged as its greatest leverage in negotiations with Washington.

Moreover, Iran has been inflicting enormous economic costs on the region and the global economy. As a result, Gulf leaders are eager for a deal that avoids further escalation and leads to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas is usually exported.

However, for Radboy, it is not just the war that needs to come to a close, but also the calls for the destruction of Iran from her fellow Iranians.

“I have watched people become so consumed by hatred of the Islamic Republic that they seem willing to sacrifice Iran itself. [In their view] civilians can die, the economy can collapse and infrastructure can be destroyed as long as it weakens the government,” she says.

articles.title: Israeli fire kills three in Gaza City during reported raid, medics say
articles.summary: Unconfirmed local reports say the Israeli military carried out air and artillery strikes after a raid by an Israel-backed militia was discovered.
articles.body:
At least two Palestinian children and a woman have been killed by Israeli fire in western Gaza City, Palestinian medics say.

Unconfirmed local reports say that an Israel-backed Palestinian militia carried out a raid and that the Israeli military carried out shelling and air strikes after it was discovered.

A third child was killed in a separate incident in central Gaza.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said that a senior Hamas official had been arrested, but it was not clear whether the announcement was related to the incident in Gaza City.

Videos from Gaza City captured chaotic scenes, with the sound of gunfire and the aftermath of air strikes.

Initial Palestinian reports said that a special Israeli unit infiltrated a crowded area using a van and motorcycles.

It is not clear whether those involved were Israeli forces or members of an Israel-backed Palestinian militia.

A local source told the BBC that a senior Hamas security official was believed to have been targeted.

The Israeli military reportedly carried out drone strikes to try to secure the special unit after its presence was uncovered.

The military has only confirmed striking several targets in Gaza "in order to remove threats to the security forces", adding that there were no injuries to its troops.

articles.title: Is recalled Argentine beef connected to Trump’s beef import plan?
articles.summary: The recalled beef is not part of the president’s plan to bring down prices by importing foreign beef.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Was a recall for nearly 30,000 pounds of raw Argentine beef related to President Trump’s plan to import more beef ?

In an effort to bring down beef prices , Trump suspended some tariffs in order to import 300,000 metric tons of ground beef from foreign sources.

The move has been opposed by cattle ranchers and led to rumors about the source of the meat .

The U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) issued a Class I recall for the beef, which was distributed in Texas and Florida, after the shipments bypassed mandatory import reinspection.

The 29,628 pounds of raw, boneless beef were imported by Corte Argentino USA LLC and distributed to retailers and food service operators.

No illnesses have been connected to the shipment.

Routine import log audits done by federal inspectors showed that the beef entered without final federal clearance.

Meat imported to the U.S. goes through several steps, with a final FSIS reinspection of packaging, labeling, documentation, general condition and potential biological contamination.

The recall is related to that administrative failure rather than any biological pathogen or contamination.

Is the recalled beef connected to Trump’s plan?

Although rumors online have linked the two, suggesting that meat brought in under Trump’s plan has been recalled for safety reasons, there is no evidence to support those rumors.

Trump’s order halting tariffs on some foreign beef imports begins Sept. 1. The recall of Argentine beef was issued in early August.

Additionally, while many have speculated that Trump will be bringing in beef from Argentina, the White House has not specified which countries will have beef tariffs temporarily suspended. The imports could come from any number of countries from which the U.S. often imports beef.

articles.title: California’s affordability crisis threatens America’s defense industrial base
articles.summary: California's aerospace and defense manufacturing sector offers skilled trades careers paying $100,000, but the state's affordability crisis looms large.
articles.body: America is investing billions to build the world’s most advanced ships, aircraft, missiles, autonomous systems and satellites. But those investments mean little if we do not have the welders, machinists, technicians, engineers and mechanics to build and maintain them. California should be leading that effort. The state is home to more than 30 major defense installations and one of America’s most important aerospace and defense ecosystems. These industries offer skilled workers good careers – often paying $90,000 to $100,000 a year without requiring a four-year degree. AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX There is just one problem: California has made it increasingly difficult for the workers we need to afford to live here. A $100,000 salary sounds impressive until rent approaches $3,000 a month. Gasoline, electricity, insurance, food and taxes consume more of every paycheck and homeownership feels increasingly out of reach. NEWSOM TARGETS MAJOR AFFORDABILITY SQUEEZE IN ‘STRIKING’ CONVERGENCE WITH TRUMP We cannot talk seriously about California’s workforce shortage without talking about California’s affordability crisis. The defense industrial base already faces an aging workforce and a shortage of skilled tradesmen. Across America, millions of manufacturing jobs could go unfilled in the coming years as experienced workers retire and too few young Americans replace them. WANT TO STRENGTHEN AMERICA'S ECONOMY? THE KEY INVESTMENT IS HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT California cannot afford to make that challenge worse by pricing workers out of the state. The first part of the solution is getting more young Americans into the trades. SKIP TWO YEARS OF COLLEGE DEBT AND GIVE YOUR FAMILY A LIFETIME OF WEALTH For too long, our culture promoted a "college for all" mentality that treated a four-year degree as the primary measure of success. That was a mistake. College is the right choice for many Americans. It is not the only path to prosperity. Skilled trades offer something increasingly valuable: the opportunity to earn while you learn. ELITE COLLEGES ARE LOSING AMERICA’S TRUST. COMMUNITY COLLEGES CAN WIN IT BACK Instead of spending four years accumulating student debt, apprentices can begin earning immediately while developing skills employers desperately need. A young machinist, welder, diesel mechanic or heavy-equipment operator can establish a career years before many college graduates enter the workforce. A $100,000 salary sounds impressive until rent approaches $3,000 a month. Gasoline, electricity, insurance, food and taxes consume more of every paycheck and homeownership feels increasingly out of reach. Artificial intelligence may disrupt some white-collar professions. But AI is not going to weld the hull of a ship, repair a diesel engine, machine a precision component, or maintain an aircraft on a flight line. AMERICA'S AI BOOM IS A JOBS OPPORTUNITY, NOT AN EXCUSE FOR UNIVERSAL BASIC INCOME These are good jobs. They are essential jobs. And California should be competing aggressively to attract the Americans capable of doing them. The Trump administration is taking important steps nationally by challenging the outdated "college for all" model, reducing unnecessary barriers to career and technical education, expanding apprenticeships and opening additional pathways for short-term vocational training. INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE The America First Policy Institute’s "America First Workforce Agenda" similarly recognizes that rebuilding American manufacturing requires government, education and private industry to put the American worker first. But Washington cannot solve California’s problem alone. THINK YOUR STATE IS EXPENSIVE? NEW DATA REVEALS WHERE AMERICANS FACE THE HIGHEST COST-OF-LIVING Sacramento has a responsibility, too. It makes little sense to train a 22-year-old Californian for a $90,000 defense manufacturing job if that worker concludes he can afford a better home, and have lower taxes, cheaper energy and a higher quality of life by taking his skills to another state. California government must make prosperity part of its workforce strategy. That means building more housing, lowering unnecessary regulatory barriers, confronting excessive energy costs, reducing the cost of doing business, expanding career and technical education and making it easier for manufacturers to build factories and hire workers. Workforce development cannot simply mean training people. It must mean creating a state where those workers can afford to build lives and raise families. California once embodied that promise. It was the Golden State because Americans came here to build things, start businesses, raise families and pursue opportunity. Its aerospace industry helped win the Cold War and put Americans on the moon. California can lead again. Instead of spending four years accumulating student debt, apprentices can begin earning immediately while developing skills employers desperately need. A young machinist, welder, diesel mechanic or heavy-equipment operator can establish a career years before many college graduates enter the workforce. But we cannot simultaneously say we desperately need machinists, welders, mechanics and technicians while pursuing policies that make those same workers unable to afford a home near their jobs. National security and economic prosperity increasingly depend on rebuilding America’s industrial base. California possesses the installations, companies, universities, technical expertise and history to be at the center of that revival. Now it needs the workers. Parents should encourage young Americans to consider the trades. Schools should treat technical education with the respect it deserves. Industry should invest in apprenticeships and training. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION And California’s government must do its part by making the Golden State affordable and prosperous enough that the next generation of American workers actually wants – and can afford - to stay. articles.title: Florida set to carry out 14th execution this year in the nation’s busiest death chamber
articles.summary: MIAMI — A Florida man convicted of fatally shooting a 16-year-old girl who rejected his romantic advances and wounding two of her friends is set to be executed Tuesday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled this month in the state.
articles.body: MIAMI — A Florida man convicted of fatally shooting a 16-year-old girl who rejected his romantic advances and wounding two of her friends is set to be executed Tuesday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled this month in the state. Harold Gene Lucas, 74, is set to receive a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at 6 p.m. He would be the 14th prisoner put to death this year in Florida, and Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has already signed death warrants for two more executions set for later this September. Lucas chose not to file appeals with the Florida Supreme Court or the U.S. Supreme Court. He told a circuit judge after his death warrant was issued that he wanted to waive all post-conviction proceedings, and the judge granted his request several days later. “I’ve been on death row for 50 years, and I have no desire to carry this any further,” Lucas told the judge, according to court transcripts. “The sooner it’s over, the better I’ll enjoy it. I am tired.” Lucas was sentenced to death five times by two different judges Lucas was sentenced to death — and resentenced to death four more times — after being convicted of first-degree murder and two counts of attempted first-degree murder for the deadly 1976 attack on Jill Piper and the wounding of her friends, Richard Byrd Jr. and Terri Rice. According to court records, Lucas was 24 in August 1976 when he was arrested for trespassing at Piper’s Bonita Springs home, south of Fort Myers. Lucas had known the teen for four years and worked for her family, officials said. Lucas and Piper had previously dated, and Lucas told a friend that he planned to marry the girl. About a week after the arrest, Lucas and Piper had two separate confrontations on the same day, several hours apart, investigators said. Witnesses testified that Lucas threatened to kill Piper. Piper asked Byrd and Rice to spend that night at her home for protection, officials said. Lucas eventually showed up with a rifle and shot Piper multiple times while she begged for her life and then shot and wounded her friends, investigators said. Lucas was arrested the next day. Lucas was initially sentenced to death in 1977 with a 12-0 jury recommendation, court records show. The Florida Supreme Court later ruled that the trial judge was wrong to consider the heinousness of the attempted murders while deciding the sentence for the murder. That same trial judge resentenced Lucas to death in 1980. By the time a third sentencing was ordered, the original trial judge had passed away, and a new judge was assigned. That judge sentenced Lucas to death in 1985, but the Florida Supreme Court later ruled that a new jury should hear the case, though the conviction itself would continue to stand. The new jury recommended death by 11-1, and Lucas was sentenced to death for a fourth time in 1987. The Florida Supreme Court ruled the sentencing order wasn’t clear, and that second judge sentenced Lucas to death for a fifth and final time in 1990. No appeals after that were successful. Florida leads the way in executions A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Florida led the way with 19 lethal injections, a record in the state since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida has carried out more than half of the 23 total executions in the U.S. this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Two more executions are planned in Florida later this month. Daniel Owen Conahan Jr., 72, is scheduled to die on Sept. 10, followed by Curtis Wilkie Beasley, 77, on Sept. 29. Conahan was convicted of kidnapping and strangling a man he had paid to pose for nude photos, and authorities suspect him of similar homicides committed in the 1990s in southwest Florida. Beasley was convicted of beating a woman to death with a hammer, robbing her and stealing her car in 1995. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

articles.title: SC quashes FIRs against all NEET protesters, but 'hardened criminals' to face trial; CJP reacts
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday invoked its special powers and quashed all FIRs registered against student protesters in different parts of the co.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday invoked its special powers and quashed all FIRs registered against student protesters in different parts of the country during the NEET paper leak protests.The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana said the order had been passed in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and shall not be treated as a precedent.The apex court said it was invoking its special powers under Article 142 of the Constitution considering the future of the students who bona fide participated in the protests.The court, however, allowed Delhi Police to pursue the FIR against 2,873 individuals who were present at the Jantar Mantar protests, citing their serious criminal antecedents.This comes a day after the Centre moved the apex court seeking to quash FIRs registered against student protesters over alleged violence during protests against the NEET paper leak in Delhi and other states.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre and Delhi Police, also informed the apex court that the Centre remained committed to fulfilling all three assurances given to CJP leaders during their meeting with the government.Under the first assurance, the Centre would not pursue FIRs registered between July 20 and July 25. The second was that no fresh FIRs would be registered in connection with the matter.The third assurance was that the government would provide compensation to the families of students who died by suicide allegedly in connection with the NEET paper leak."The Centre is committed to honouring the assurance given to CJP leaders to provide compensation to the families of students who died by suicide after the NEET exam cancellation; however, three months are needed to work out the modalities," Mehta told the Supreme Court."As of now, we are committed to fulfilling all three assurances," he added.Following the apex court hearing, Cockroach Janata Party called off its September 5 protest against the Centre for failing to honour the promises made to persuade the group to withdraw the agitation."I want to state that in view of the positive assurances of the Government of India and the judicial sanctity bestowed upon them today, and in view of the order being passed by this court, the CJP deems it appropriate to withdraw the call for the march on September 5 and looks forward to compliance with today's order," CJP co-convener Sourav Das said during a hearing in the Supreme Court.How CJP reactedAfter the hearing, Das said welcomed SC's order but also questioned why were these 'hardend criminals' allowed to roam freely in the society in the first place."Regarding the Delhi Police’s apprehension, based on facial recognition technology, that around 2,800 alleged hardened criminals were present at the protest site, we argued during negotiations with the government that if these 2,800 hardened criminals were indeed present, the first question was why they were roaming freely in society in the first place," Das said while talking to reporters."Secondly, if they committed any heinous crimes, such as rape, murder, or other grave offences, at the protest site, then they should be prosecuted, investigated, and imprisoned," he added.During a hearing on August 18 on petitions related to the student protests, Supreme Court had indicated that it was inclined to quash the FIRs by exercising its special powers under Article 142 of the Constitution.The indication came after the court was informed of legal complications in withdrawing the FIRs. Once registered, the cases can be closed only through a closure report, which the concerned Magistrate has the discretion to reject.Earlier, Supreme Court had also constituted a committee to examine allegations of excessive use of force by security personnel against students during the July 20 march over the NEET paper leak.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
